articles.title: AI refutes 30-year-old mathematical assumption in computer science
articles.summary: A central tenet in computer science has apparently been disproven by OpenAI, a result that will force textbooks to be rewritten if it is confirmed
articles.content:
A central tenet in computer science has apparently been disproven by OpenAI, a result that will force textbooks to be rewritten if it is confirmed

OpenAI announced three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, claims its AI models have disproven the exponential time hypothesis – a fundamental assumption that underpins computer science.

“This came as a complete surprise, a shock,” says Fedor Fomin at the University of Bergen in Norway. “Nobody I know expected it.”

Proposed nearly 30 years ago, the exponential time hypothesis (ETH) tries to put a limit on how quickly computers can solve certain logical puzzles.

Advertisement

The simplest way would be to try every possible combination of true or false for each part of the puzzle. ETH proposes that, although it may be possible to do this quicker with shortcuts, the amount of work needed has to grow exponentially as the puzzle gets bigger.

OpenAI, however, says its models have devised an algorithm that can beat the previously assumed speed limit for solving logical puzzles, apparently proving ETH false. “Assuming that it is confirmed, this is an enormous breakthrough,” says Leslie Goldberg at the University of Oxford.

Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter

Many computer science findings assume ETH is true. If it isn’t, the conclusions they establish about computational limits become useless. “It would require a complete revision of several areas of algorithms and complexity,” says Fomin, who says a textbook he wrote on the subject would become obsolete if the finding holds.

ETH is linked to a long-standing maths problem known as P versus NP, which concerns whether a problem whose answer is easy to check is also easy to solve. If ETH were true, it would have implied that the answer was no. But disproving ETH wouldn’t mean the answer is yes. “This doesn’t have a direct impact on P versus NP, so we should not view it as progress towards P versus NP,” says Goldberg.

The result was announced alongside other breakthroughs in maths and physics in a blog post on 26 October.

In mathematics, OpenAI says its AI has proved a 1991 conjecture that waves cannot remain intensely focused for long. If confirmed, this would also answer enduring questions about how thin a shape can be while also containing line segments that point in every direction, as well as how waves spread.

In theoretical physics, OpenAI claims to have proven that quantum field theories – including quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong force holding quarks together – make sense mathematically, rather than just producing predictions that match experiments. The findings also touch on the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory, part of a million-dollar mathematical problem, but don’t resolve the entire challenge. That work hasn’t been released publicly while an external group led by Nobel laureate David Gross examines it.

OpenAI says it verified the ETH result using Lean, a piece of software that checks mathematical proofs. Stefan Szeider at TU Wien in Austria has looked at what OpenAI has released and says he expects it to withstand scrutiny, although he says researchers still need to check that the formally proven statement means what its authors say it means.

To do so, OpenAI has commissioned an independent group, including Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, both at the University of California, San Diego, who helped propose ETH, to examine the findings. In an open letter, the group says it could “change an important part of theoretical computer science”.

The speed at which AI is solving maths problems and the way AI firms are releasing their findings have concerned some academics. Magnus Wahlström at Royal Holloway, University of London, describes the phenomenon as “mathematics done by press”, worrying that proprietary models can suddenly overturn months of researchers’ work.

Bart Jansen at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands describes OpenAI’s work on ETH as “ingenious”, “spectacular” and “awe-inspiring – but also humbling.” “It really makes you think about the future of mathematics, algorithms and academia,” he says.

Clément Canonne at the University of Sydney says proving something and understanding why it is true aren’t the same thing. “The web collapsed, and we looked behind,” he says of the network of findings relying on ETH. “We have no idea why yet.”

OpenAI says it is experimenting with an approach in which independent academics organise efforts to verify and explain the results. But Fomin welcomes the disruption. “This result destroys a lot, but it also opens many new opportunities and new questions that nobody expected,” he says. “One shouldn’t complain about having too many interesting mathematical breakthroughs to try to digest,” says Wahlström.

This has broad significance for the field of computer science and mathematics, potentially rewriting textbooks and opening new research directions. The discovery is well-contextualized with expert opinions, verification efforts, and implications, showing substantial substance and real-world impact on scientific knowledge.

articles.title: Student Makers, a deeper dive: bringing free STEM to students on three continents
articles.summary:

The post Student Makers, a deeper dive: bringing free STEM to students on three continents first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

This article kicks off The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under.

It was winter break, and Dilan Mehta had time on his hands. His dad was packing for a mission trip to Kenya, where he’d been volunteering with Kenya Relief, a medical organization that runs a school in Migori, for years. Dilan packed a bag of stuffed animals for the children there. Then he glanced at his 3D printer.

He started designing LEGO-inspired sets, printing each one out, and tucking them in alongside the stuffed animals. Somewhere between one print and the next, a different thought took shape. The school had students who could use a curriculum, and his dad had room in a suitcase.

That’s how a 3D printer ended up in Migori, Kenya, and why it’s still being used to teach students today.

What is Student Makers?

Student Makers is a nonprofit that offers free STEM workshops to students across the United States, Kenya, and India, and every instructor is a former student. Most of them are still in high school.

The organization was founded in California in 2019 by Anthony Neil Tan, then a high school senior. There was no space at his school where students interested in technology and making could come together to learn, so he built one. He called it the Maker Hub Club Initiative, secured a $5,000 grant from a social impact scholarship, and got it off the ground. The framework was three steps: learn a skill, make a project, showcase it. He was in his first year of college when he started handing it off.

Serve: the fourth pillar

Dilan didn’t find Student Makers; rather, Anthony found him. Roughly six years ago, Dilan was only in 8th grade and had entered an Autodesk design contest with a 3D-printed fingerboard, one that used flexible filament on the grip surface to behave like rubber. Anthony came across it and reached out. Would Dilan want to join a group where students build things and learn from each other?

He joined, took the 3D printing course, came back as an instructor, and eventually rebuilt the entire curriculum from scratch around design thinking rather than output. A few years later, he was running the organization.

But he felt that the project’s mission needed some rethinking. The original framework had three steps: learn, make, showcase. Dilan added a fourth, serve, because the workshops were primarily reaching students who already had resources, and that wasn’t what he’d signed up for. His dad’s Kenya-bound suitcase gave him the opening for a bigger idea to launch.

Teaching through rain and static

When Dilan sent that 3D printer to Kenya Relief Academy, he wasn’t thinking about it as a program. He was thinking about a school with 800 students, roughly 170 to 190 of them orphaned children, consistently ranked the top primary school in its region out of more than 800, and without any STEM infrastructure. His dad’s Kenya Relief contacts connected him to the teachers there, and he started meeting with them remotely three times a week.

Every session ran over video call, Dilan in the US and the teachers in Migori, and when the Wi-Fi dropped, which it often would, they’d wait, reconnect, and keep going. He trained them in Autodesk Fusion 360, Tinkercad, and 3D printer operation, working through how to teach all of it to a classroom he’s never seen in person.

“They constantly have Wi-Fi issues,” Dilan said. “Anytime there’s rain, they basically lose connection. Just being patient, being empathetic, understanding that that’s just the situation.”

Ruth Agongo, a teacher at Kenya Relief Academy, described what it looked like from the other end. “You are a game-changer,” she said. “Whatever you have taught us, we are putting into action because the kids are really excited by the technology.”

Jacob

A few semesters into his time at Georgia Tech, once Dilan had actually taken a step back from Student Makers and was serving mostly as an advisory board member, Dilan got a message from the teachers at Kenya Relief Academy. They needed help with a science fair project: an Arduino-based robot that could navigate a garden, measure soil moisture at different points, and decide where to water.

Dilan didn’t know much about robotics, but he was at Georgia Tech, so he asked around. Twelve students from the university ended up on the project. They built components in Atlanta while the Kenya team built in Migori, troubleshot over video call, and sent physical supplies through a similar suitcase network that had carried the original printer.

That team placed third at regionals of the Kenya Science and Engineering Fair. One of the students on it, a ninth-grader named Jacob, now leads Kenya Relief Academy’s robotics team. His dream is to become a rocket engineer at NASA.

A family connection in India

Rohan Naegle, who led Student Makers before the current team took over, brought a similar program to Dr. R.V. Shah English Medium School in rural Gujarat, India, after his grandfather put him in touch with the school. Live 3D printing classes run there over video call, using the same structure. More than 25 secondary students have completed the program, and a donated printer stays at the school. Both the Kenya and India connections came organically, through family.

How the pipeline runs

Aarush Goel, who now leads the high school chapters, came in the same way Dilan did: a friend pulled him in to co-teach a Python workshop, and he showed up not entirely sure what he was doing. “You just start teaching and everything goes into place,” he said. He’s since led five workshop tracks across the US, and next year he’ll start a Student Makers chapter at his own college.

Instructors are recruited the same way at every level. At the end of each cycle, a call goes out for anyone who wants to come back and teach the next round. Usually one or two students say yes. They already know the program from the inside, which tends to make them good at the part that matters most: building something new students actually want to stay in.

Anthony, watching from his current advisory role, put it plainly. “It’s more relatable, a high schooler showing a middle schooler how to do some 3D printing than someone who’s already a young adult,” he said. “So it’s nice keeping that peer-to-peer instruction model.” He’s 25. The organization he started as a high school senior just turned seven.

Growing the network

Student Makers recently joined a partnership with Youth Technology Corps Global Alliance, a network of schools across roughly 12 countries that has been running a similar peer-learning model since 1998. YTC has been doing this for nearly three decades and has school connections worldwide; Student Makers brings the volunteers and the curriculum. This fall, programs are launching under the partnership in Mexico, Colombia, Ethiopia, and Illinois, with the 3D printing and CAD curriculum going into Mexico specifically.

“I would have never imagined that we would have this extensive of a reach,” Anthony said. The reach he couldn’t have imagined started with a simple observation: students interested in technology and making didn’t have a space to come together. So he built one.

Why Student Makers opens this year’s series

Each year, The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers series runs in the weeks before Thanksgiving, and this year, for the first time, every person in it is 30 or under. When Aarush reached out to us with the Student Makers story last summer, we spent weeks talking with the people who built this organization and were honestly floored by their dedication, hard work, and willingness to serve others.

The five other changemakers in this year’s series were nominated by The Optimist Daily community, but Student Makers was not. It was the story that inspired the decision behind this year’s “30 and under” theme.

This article skims the surface of the deeper story behind Student Makers. If you want to learn more about their incredible work, hang tight for a podcast episode featuring the voices behind this initiative. It’ll be coming out in early 2027. In the meantime, you can learn more and support their work at www.studentmakers.org.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

articles.title: Preprint-centric publishing approach gets major boost
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03445-wEuropean funders put weight behind controversial ‘publish, review, curate’ model for preprints.
articles.content:
The Open Research Europe platform offers 2.5 million researchers full editorial services on the platform at no charge.Credit: Michael Szebor/Nature

Science funders and research organizations in Europe are joining forces to expand open-access publishing and make the peer-review process more transparent, with the aim of spurring change in scholarly communication.

By early November, the European Commission will roll out an expanded version of its Open Research Europe (ORE) platform, which uses a ‘publish, review, curate’ model. In this approach, preprints are posted, reviewed openly — with the identity of the reviewers and their reports made public — then flagged as ‘peer reviewed’ on the same platform.

Joining the ORE are funders from 11 countries, including the German Research Foundation DFG and the Swiss National Science Foundation, as well as three major research organizations, including the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). More than 2.5 million researchers will now receive full editorial services on the platform at no charge. Since its launch in 2021, ORE has published some 1,500 articles.

“This is a collective effort to build a more transparent, sustainable publishing system that serves the research community and society as a whole,” says Karla Anaya-Carlsson, who chairs the ORE Funders Group and is based in Stockholm.

A big burden?

Mario Malički, a metascientist at Stanford University in California, says that the platform simplifies publishing for researchers and reduces funders’ costs. But, he cautions, running something at that scale “becomes a major undertaking of who runs the checks, who curates it and makes the final decisions”.

The expanded project has a budget of €16 million (US$17.7 million) between now and 2030, 60% of which will be provided by the European Commission and the remainder coming from the other funders and research organizations. It will be governed by these bodies, and hosted and operated by CERN, Europe’s particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland.

Independently of the expansion of ORE, a group of 40 funders, institutions, publishers and platforms announced on 28 October the creation of the Publish, Review, Curate Alliance to promote such open publishing initiatives. Members include the journal eLife, the preprint organization OpenRxiv and the archiving service Europe PubMed Central. Other members include funders such as the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the Gates Foundation, and institutional libraries at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and the University of Cambridge, UK.

Radical approach

The ‘publish, review, curate’ system was implemented by eLife in late 2022 and caused controversy. Some saw the system as a threat to the reputation of the journal, saying that the possibility of rejecting manuscripts during the peer-review process is key to integrity and consistency. Others lauded the model as the future of research publishing.

Within two years of adopting this model, eLife lost its impact factor. Some bibliographic databases, including Web of Science, changed the way the journal was indexed. The finer details of how indexing services will respond to the expansion of ORE are not yet clear; ORE also has no impact factor, nor will it seek one.

ORE curates the literature by putting papers into collections based on topic or funding mechanism. This differs fromat eLife, for example, where editors add one-word assessments, such as ‘fundamental’, ‘useful’, ‘compelling’ or ‘inadequate’, to signal to readers the significance of a study and the strength of evidence.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant, large-scale initiative to improve scholarly publishing by expanding an open-access, transparent peer-review platform that benefits millions of researchers and the broader society by promoting open science and reducing barriers to knowledge dissemination.
articles.personality_title: Europe expands open-access platform to transform research publishing
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many scientific articles are shared before official review as 'preprints,' but the process of checking and approving them can be unclear. Europe aims to change this by making research publishing more open and fair.

**What happened** – The European Commission and research funders from 11 countries are expanding the Open Research Europe (ORE) platform by early November 2026. This platform lets scientists post their work openly, have it reviewed publicly with reviewers’ names and reports visible, and then mark it as peer-reviewed on the same site. Over 2.5 million researchers will now get free editorial services through ORE. The platform is backed by a €16 million budget and run by CERN, the European physics lab.

**Impact** – This approach makes it easier and cheaper for researchers to publish their work while making the review process transparent. Unlike traditional journals where reviews are secret, ORE shows reviews openly, which can build trust and speed up sharing. It also helps many researchers avoid paywalls or delays common in regular publishing.

**What's next step** – The platform will continue growing with support from many organizations, including a new alliance promoting this open publishing model. The effects on how research is counted or ranked in databases are still being watched, but ORE will focus on helping scientists share and improve their work rather than chasing impact scores.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Europe’s expanded Open Research Europe platform offers millions of scientists free, transparent publishing services that could change how research is shared and reviewed worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: L'Europe étend une plateforme en libre accès pour transformer la publication scientifique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux articles scientifiques sont partagés avant la revue officielle sous forme de « prépublications », mais le processus de vérification peut être flou. L'Europe souhaite rendre la publication scientifique plus ouverte et équitable.

Contrairement aux revues traditionnelles où les évaluations sont secrètes, ORE les montre publiquement, ce qui peut renforcer la confiance et accélérer le partage. Elle aide aussi de nombreux chercheurs à éviter les barrières financières ou les retards habituels.

articles.title: Would you trust an emergency alert written by AI?
articles.content:
This story was produced by Grist and co-published with WIRED . It is part of Distorted , a Grist series exploring the spread of misinformation in the wake of extreme weather, and is published with support from the CO2 Foundation.​​ ​​

Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety, and she talks to state and local emergency managers around her region all the time. The meteorologist told Myers that a local emergency manager had published a graphic showing where Isaias might threaten the Alabama coast with a “sting jet” of high winds.

The problem? The emergency manager had generated the graphic using an artificial intelligence chatbot, and it wasn’t accurate.

“That county emergency manager was trying to get his stakeholders to focus on the risk in that county, and so he had asked AI to help him,” she said. “It did what he wanted it to do, but it was not meteorologically accurate.”

Most emergency management agencies don’t permit employees to use generative AI, but Myers and most other emergency management experts agree that its usage is likely already pervasive at state and local disaster departments. There are hundreds of companies that are marketing AI tools to emergency managers for tasks like flood damage assessment and resource coordination, but public communication is one of the areas where government employees and startups have the most interest.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The reason? Most emergency managers aren’t very good at sending out alerts and quickly communicating about disasters with the public. That’s not because they’re emergency managers, but because they are human beings. They tend to write in jargon that non-experts might not understand, leave out information on the assumption that the public already knows it, and include irrelevant details that could distract people from what they actually do need to know.

“A lot of agencies are really limited in resources and the number of people that they have,” said Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who has created a comprehensive dashboard that provides templates for disaster alerts. “I think they recognize it as a priority, but they don’t prioritize it until they realize they should have. They’re just trying to get their job done without screwing something up.”

Emergency department personnel with the city of New York monitor the watch-command room in Brooklyn on February 23, 2026, ahead of a winter storm.

Matthew Hoen / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Emergency managers are the government officials who are in charge of disaster response and recovery. At the state and local level, It is these officials and their agencies, not the Federal Emergency Management Agency, that make up the first line of defense after an extreme weather event. As such, emergency managers often like to say that “trust is our currency,” and it’s in their communication with the public that they build and lose this trust.

As climate disasters become more frequent and widespread, there have been numerous examples of flawed human communication scrambling an emergency response. In 2016, for instance, adjacent counties in California issued a “voluntary evacuation” and a “mandatory evacuation” for the same wildfire. In Australia in 2019, officials warned about wildfires by using the phrase “Watch and Act,” which the government later said caused “significant confusion” because no one knew what it meant.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

In some cases, inadequate communication can mean the difference between life and death. This happened in Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire. A few weeks after the fire, a heavy rainstorm produced a deadly mudslide. The government of Santa Barbara County struggled to communicate the risk to residents still traumatized from the blaze and experiencing a phenomenon that Sutton calls “warning fatigue.” The county sent alerts to everyone in the “voluntary evacuation zone” for wildfires, telling residents to “stay alert to changing conditions and be prepared to leave immediately.” Most of those residents should have left immediately, but to many the evacuation notice was optional; others just didn’t want to evacuate for a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others.

Governments that put out bad warnings are apt to lose the public’s trust said Sutton. “They’re losing the opportunity to be that voice to help people to be safe.”

After a series of erroneous evacuation alerts to L.A. residents sparked panic during an active wildfire season in January 2025, the director of the county’s emergency management department apologized.

Chris Delmas / AFP via Getty Images

In theory, alerts are a perfect use case for artificial intelligence, and in particular for the generative AI systems that have developed at a dramatic pace over the past few years. FEMA provides training sessions for emergency managers to learn best practices for synthesizing and sending alerts, but many officials don’t remember all their training when an emergency arrives. A large language model is different. It can read hundreds of thousands of alerts in mere minutes, digest all the research on what works in similar scenarios, and then apply that to edit a human alert in seconds.

“If you’ve only sent one [alert] in your life, and that was 15 years ago, and you need to remember all your training, and you’re thinking ‘Hey, there’s a chemical plume coming my way, the phone’s ringing, the radio’s blaring, I need help,’ the AI is probably gonna do a better job than you are,” said Rob Dale, a former meteorologist who now runs the emergency management department in Ingham County, Michigan.

Dale has already used AI to draft a few practice alerts behind the scenes, but he’s never had to send one out. Ingham County is a small county in central Michigan, and it’s immune from major weather events like hurricanes and fires. If such an event did happen, Dale said he would have no issue allowing a chatbot to draft his incident communication, but he’d still want control over sending the alert out.

Some experts believe the technology is already good enough to deploy. EM1, a startup that produces AI software for emergency managers, has used Sutton’s research to train a model that its executives say is already better than almost any human emergency manager. The company has tested this in-house model on a number of scenarios including wildfires and tsunamis. It can already match or exceed human capabilities on most benchmark tests.

Sutton gave Grist an example of how the software works: Grist provided her with a recent alert sent by a New Mexico county that was trying to warn residents about flooding on the San Juan River.

The original alert “Breeched banks. The water is rising. EVACUATE NOW. McGee Park open for people and pets, RV.” 1 of 1

Sutton asked the EM1 model to evaluate and revise the alert. In a few seconds, it produced what she said is a far better alert, one that checks all the main boxes of disaster communication.

The new alert “San Juan County: Floodwater is rising near [location]. People in [evacuation area]: LEAVE NOW for higher ground. Do not walk or drive through floodwater. McGee Park is open for people and pets. Check [official update source] for updates.” 1 of 1

The model identified and fixed several problems with the original text, which does not say who is sending the alert, name the specific location where flooding is happening, or clarify who needs to evacuate and give advice on how to do so safely. It misspells the word “breached,” and it doesn’t provide any guidance on where residents can seek further information.

EM1 has contracts with around a hundred government agencies and school districts, but none are using it to automate their extreme weather alerts just yet. For the moment, they’re only using it to workshop plans and internal preparations. Even so, all the experts interviewed for this story said they are certain that many emergency managers are already using chatbots to write messages, even if they won’t admit it. Sutton said that the emergency managers who take her alert training sessions often present her with high-quality alerts they have drafted in seconds using ChatGPT or Gemini.

“Official adoption is pretty low, but people are unofficially using it, absolutely,” said Sarah Miller, a professor of emergency management at Pierce College in Florida and a longtime instructor at the National Disaster Preparedness Training Center. “They’re using their own personal accounts, or they’re using free ones.”

It sounds like an easy trade-off: if AI is better and faster than humans, and the difference between a good alert and a bad alert can be life and death, we should be using AI for every heat wave and wildfire. Yet even researchers who are bullish on chatbot technology say that making the switch could backfire. Members of the public who are skeptical of AI or who don’t trust the government in the first place may spurn agencies that publish AI-generated graphics or social media posts. In Syracuse, New York, for instance, a union of public employees sued the local government for using an AI service to answer non-emergency 911 calls.

“We trust things that we perceive [are] authentic and care about us,” said Ginny Katz, the founder of HazAdapt, a consultancy that helps disaster officials figure out how to use technology. “AI-generated content does not feel authentic.” There’s also a risk that chatbots could allow emergency managers to send out more alerts, and faster, which could increase the risk of warning fatigue.

As is the case in other areas where AI is being deployed, disaster experts say that for the moment the software is only as capable as the person using it. A seasoned emergency manager might be able to speed up their communication with the public by having a chatbot draft a series of alerts, but an inexperienced one rushing to create an urgent alert won’t know how to evaluate the output of a model like ChatGPT or Claude.

Even though the technology is a ways off from being able to perform without a human expert in the loop, that hasn’t stopped many understaffed emergency management departments from using it. As for how the proliferation of AI-generated content is affecting public trust in government, experts say it’s too early to tell.

“If you had a human sending you a text message versus a computer sending you a text message, which one would you believe is being more accurate?” said Justin Snair, the founder of Preppr, another company that offers AI software to emergency managers.

The answer, he said, depends on the person receiving it.

It highlights the potential for AI to save lives by producing clearer, more accurate alerts faster than humans, addressing a significant societal need amid increasing climate disasters. The story is focused, detailed, and relevant to a broad public interest in disaster preparedness and technology innovation.
articles.personality_title: AI shows promise in improving emergency alerts during disasters
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Emergency managers are responsible for sending warnings during disasters like hurricanes and floods. However, these alerts are often confusing or unclear because writing them quickly and clearly is very hard, especially when people are stressed or have little experience.

**What happened** – Recently, some emergency managers started using artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots to help write alerts. For example, a local emergency manager in Alabama used AI to create a graphic warning about Hurricane Isaias, but the AI-made graphic was inaccurate. Despite this, experts believe AI can help produce clearer and faster alerts by learning from thousands of past warnings.

**Impact** – Using AI could make emergency alerts better and faster, helping people understand what to do during dangerous events. For instance, an AI tool improved a flood alert by adding clear instructions and specific locations, which the original alert missed. This is important because good communication can save lives, especially as climate disasters become more common.

**What's next step** – While some emergency departments are testing AI tools, no agencies have fully switched to using AI for official alerts yet. Experts say AI should assist humans, not replace them, since people must check that AI messages are accurate. Also, public trust is key, and some worry that AI messages might feel less personal or cause alert fatigue.

**One-sentence takeaway** – AI is becoming a useful tool to help emergency managers create clearer, faster alerts, but human oversight and public trust remain essential for its success.

articles.personality_title_es: La IA promete mejorar las alertas de emergencia durante desastres
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los gestores de emergencias son responsables de enviar advertencias durante desastres como huracanes e inundaciones. Sin embargo, estas alertas a menudo son confusas o poco claras porque redactarlas rápido y bien es difícil, especialmente cuando la gente está estresada o sin experiencia.

**Qué pasó** – Recientemente, algunos gestores de emergencias comenzaron a usar chatbots de inteligencia artificial (IA) para ayudar a redactar las alertas. Por ejemplo, un gestor local en Alabama usó IA para crear un gráfico sobre el huracán Isaias, pero el gráfico no fue preciso. A pesar de esto, los expertos creen que la IA puede producir alertas más claras y rápidas al aprender de miles de advertencias pasadas.

**Impacto** – Usar IA podría hacer que las alertas de emergencia sean mejores y más rápidas, ayudando a la gente a entender qué hacer en situaciones peligrosas. Por ejemplo, una herramienta de IA mejoró una alerta de inundación al añadir instrucciones claras y lugares específicos, algo que la alerta original no tenía. Esto es importante porque una buena comunicación puede salvar vidas, especialmente con el aumento de desastres climáticos.

**Próximo paso** – Aunque algunos departamentos de emergencia están probando estas herramientas de IA, ninguna agencia las usa oficialmente para enviar alertas aún. Los expertos dicen que la IA debe ayudar a los humanos, no reemplazarlos, ya que las personas deben verificar que los mensajes de IA sean correctos. Además, la confianza del público es clave, y algunos temen que los mensajes de IA parezcan menos personales o causen cansancio por tantas alertas.

**Resumen en una frase** – La IA se está convirtiendo en una herramienta útil para ayudar a gestores de emergencias a crear alertas más claras y rápidas, pero la supervisión humana y la confianza pública siguen siendo esenciales.
